opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I go back and forth on. My view is that fine-tuning isn't going away, but its role is shifting.

A few years ago, fine-tuning was basically the default. You'd take a pretrained backbone and adapt it to your task because the base model just couldn't do what you needed out of the box. Today the foundation models are so capable, and so good at following instructions, that a lot of what used to require fine-tuning can be handled with prompting, a few in-context examples, or some clever conditioning. For many general-purpose tasks, the ceiling of the base model rises faster than the gains you'd get from tuning a smaller one.

That said, I think fine-tuning stays very useful in a few places. One is specificity. If you care about a particular visual style, a brand identity, a specific person or product, or a domain that just isn't well represented in web-scale data, like certain kinds of medical or scientific imagery, you need to inject that information somehow. Lightweight methods like LoRA and adapters have made that cheap and practical, and I see that continuing.

The second is control and alignment. A lot of the most important work on image models after pretraining is really fine-tuning: aligning to human preferences, improving aesthetics, getting text rendering right, making the model follow complex prompts faithfully. That post-training stage is where much of the quality people perceive actually comes from, and I don't see it disappearing.

The third is efficiency. If you're deploying at scale, distilling or fine-tuning a smaller model for a narrow task can be far cheaper and faster than calling a huge general model every time.

So long term, I'd say fine-tuning becomes less of an everyday tool for end users solving generic problems, and more of a specialized instrument, for model builders shaping behavior and for people with really specific data or constraints. The open question for me is how far in-context learning can go for visual concepts. If you can show a model a handful of images and have it truly internalize a new concept without any weight updates, that changes the picture a lot. We're seeing early signs of that, but we're not fully there yet.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning can provide specificity for a particular visual style, brand identity, or specific person or product.

r002.rationale: It says that long term fine-tuning will be less of an everyday tool for generic problems, as prompting and in-context examples can handle many tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think fine-tuning is going to stay useful for a long time, but the reason it's useful is shifting. A few years ago you fine-tuned because the base model just couldn't do the thing you needed. Now the big models are broad enough that most people can get surprisingly far with prompting and in-context examples. So the question becomes: when does it still pay to actually move the weights?

I see roughly three cases that aren't going away. The first is distribution shift that's genuinely out of the pretraining data. Medical imaging, satellite, industrial inspection, scientific microscopy. Those domains have visual statistics the base model has seen very little of, and no amount of clever prompting substitutes for exposure. Second is control and consistency. If you're a product team and you need the same style, the same character, the same output format every time, fine-tuning gives you a reliability that prompting doesn't. That's where things like LoRA and adapters have really earned their keep, because you can get that control cheaply and swap it in and out. And third is cost. A large general model is expensive to serve, and a smaller model fine-tuned for your narrow task is often both cheaper and better on that task. That trade-off doesn't disappear just because the frontier models get stronger.

What I think does change is the shape of fine-tuning. It's becoming less about training a model and more about editing one. Parameter-efficient methods, preference tuning on top of a frozen backbone, teaching a vision-language model a new vocabulary or a new tool rather than retraining its perception. And honestly, the line between fine-tuning and data curation is blurring. The hard part is rarely the optimization step. It's deciding what the model should see, how to measure whether it got better, and how to avoid quietly degrading all the capabilities you weren't looking at.

So my long-term view is that fine-tuning won't be the default first move the way it was, but it'll remain the thing you reach for when you need the model to be specifically yours, or specifically small, or specifically reliable. And those needs are pretty durable.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning can provide consistent style and the same character, describing improved fidelity to a particular visual identity.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning will not be the default first move because prompting and in-context examples now work for many needs, suggesting it may be less necessary over time.

astra-6.text:
I think fine-tuning will continue to be useful, even as the base models get stronger. There’s a distinction between a model that has broad visual understanding and one that does exactly what you need in a particular application. You might care about very subtle differences between images, or work with imagery that looks quite different from the data the model was trained on.

For vision-language models, you can express some of that through prompting, which is very powerful. But language isn’t always the easiest way to specify a visual distinction. Sometimes showing the model examples of what matters is much more effective than trying to describe it.

So I think the role of fine-tuning will evolve. We may need less data and update fewer parameters, but there will still be value in adapting a general-purpose model to a particular task, domain, or user’s needs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting models to tasks, domains, and user needs, but does not identify fine-tuning as improving fidelity to a specific visual identity, character, or brand look.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning will continue to be useful, though it may require less data and fewer updated parameters. It does not suggest fine-tuning may become less necessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think fine-tuning will continue to be useful, even as the base models get much better. There’s a distinction between having a model that understands a broad range of images and having one that does exactly what you need in a particular application. You might have a specialized domain, a different data distribution, or a very specific notion of what makes an answer correct.

The interesting question is how much adaptation you need. Can you get there with prompting or a few examples, or do you need to update the model? As models improve, some tasks will move into that first category. But I’d expect there to remain applications where fine-tuning gives you better accuracy, more consistent behavior, or lets you use a smaller model. So I see it remaining part of the toolkit, with the way we use it evolving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses application-specific adaptation and improved accuracy, but does not identify fine-tuning as a way to match a particular visual identity, such as characters or a brand’s look.

r002.rationale: It says that as models improve, some tasks will shift to prompting or examples instead of updating the model, indicating fine-tuning may be less necessary for those tasks over time.
